summary.text: Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance polymath who formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun, rather than Earth, at its center.
His book On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres, published just before his death in 1543, triggered the Copernican Revolution and contributed to the Scientific Revolution.
A similar heliocentric model was developed eighteen centuries earlier by Aristarchus of Samos, but Copernicus likely arrived at his own independently.

paragraphs.heading: Putting the Sun in the middle
paragraphs.text: Nicolaus Copernicus, who lived from 1473 to 1543, worked out a model of the universe with the Sun at its centre instead of Earth. A Sun-centred picture like this is called heliocentric. He set it out in his book On the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres, which appeared shortly before he died in 1543. Its publication was a landmark in the history of science: it set off what we now call the Copernican Revolution and was a pioneering step in the Scientific Revolution.

paragraphs.heading: An old idea, reached again
paragraphs.text: Some eighteen centuries earlier, the ancient Greek astronomer Aristarchus of Samos had built a similar heliocentric model. Copernicus, though, most likely came to his own version without relying on it.

paragraphs.heading: An uncle who became a bishop
paragraphs.text: His mother's brother, Lucas Watzenrode the Younger, became his patron. Watzenrode had studied at the universities of Kraków, Cologne and Bologna. In 1489 he was elected Bishop of Warmia, although King Casimir IV had hoped to give that seat to his own son. He was a fierce enemy of the Teutonic Order, whose Grand Master once called him "the devil incarnate". From 1497 Copernicus himself served Warmia's cathedral as a canon of its chapter.

paragraphs.heading: Far more than an astronomer
paragraphs.text: Astronomy was only one of his many fields. A polymath who spoke many languages, he earned a doctorate in canon law, and worked as a mathematician, physician, classics scholar, translator, governor, diplomat and economist. In 1517 he worked out a quantity theory of money, a central idea in that field, and in 1519 he stated an economic principle that later came to be known as Gresham's law.

paragraphs.heading: A private life under watch
paragraphs.text: Copernicus never married, and no children of his are known. His sister Katharina married Barthel Gertner, a businessman and member of Thorn's city council, and Copernicus cared for her five children for the rest of his life. From at least 1531 until 1539 his ties with Anna Schilling, a housekeeper who lived in his home, were judged scandalous by two bishops of Warmia. Over several years they pressed him to end what they called his relationship with his "mistress".
